strengths: Principled theoretical formulation: the fusion objective is cleanly decomposed into grouping error and approximation error (Theorem 1), yielding an interpretable two-stage algorithm; Theorem 2 provides exact optimality for the Hungarian variant and a (9+ε)-approximation guarantee for the K-means variant under affine layers, which is a meaningful theoretical contribution rarely seen in this literature.

The framework generalizes to arbitrary differentiable architectures (MLPs, CNNs, ViTs) via the flexible 'level' abstraction, avoiding the architecture-specific adaptations required by OTFusion for transformers.

Novel and well-motivated incorporation of neuron importance/attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the fusion objective, and the paper shows this idea can be retrofitted into existing baselines (Git Re-Basin) with benefit, which strengthens the significance of the contribution beyond just the new method.

Broad and carefully designed experimental suite spanning non-IID, sharded, and full-dataset regimes, multiple split counts, two architectures (VGG11, ViT) and two datasets (CIFAR-10/100), with results averaged over multiple seeds and reported with standard deviations.

Good-faith reproducibility effort: detailed appendices cover data partitioning schemes, training hyperparameters, fusion hyperparameters (two named settings), runtime comparisons, and licenses for reused code/assets.
Honest and specific discussion of limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient variant, data-dependence of gradient fusion) rather than vague boilerplate limitations.
weaknesses: The gradient-based variant requires two very different, hand-picked hyperparameter 'settings' applied inconsistently across experiments (Setting 1 for full-dataset/sharded, Setting 2 for most non-IID cases) without a principled selection rule, which undermines claims of practical robustness/generality and complicates reproducibility for new settings.

Several baseline comparisons are incomplete: OTFusion/Git Re-Basin are only evaluated in the pairwise (2-way) case and marked N/A for 4-way/8-way splits since they are inherently pairwise, but this leaves gaps in table completeness; the intended comparison to Transformer OTFusion (Imfeld et al. 2023) could not be run due to implementation difficulties, so ViT-scale comparisons to a natural strong baseline are largely qualitative/anecdotal ("<12% accuracy").

Runtime analysis (Table 6) shows the K-means Linear variant is roughly 100x slower than OTFusion/Git Re-Basin, and this substantial computational overhead is not adequately weighed against the accuracy gains in the main text discussion of practical trade-offs.

Federated learning baselines (FedAvg, FedMA) that are discussed at length in Related Work are never empirically benchmarked, despite non-IID/federated fusion being a central motivating use case of the paper.

Ensemble performance remains a substantial upper bound not closely approached by any zero-shot fusion method in the more extreme non-IID/sharded/many-way splits, tempering the practical significance of the gains claimed.

The K-means approximation guarantee, while theoretically interesting, only applies to purely affine/linear levels and gives a fairly loose (9+ε) bound; its practical relevance for the non-linear/gradient-based variant actually used in most experiments is unclear.

Level partitioning (e.g., which layers to group for ViTs vs. VGGs) is done manually/heuristically per architecture, and the paper acknowledges this is not yet automated, limiting the 'plug-and-play' generality implied by the framing of the method as applicable to 'arbitrary layer types.'

strengths: Principled formulation: the paper cleanly decomposes the neuron-matching fusion objective into a 'grouping error' and an 'approximation error' (Theorem 1), giving an interpretable two-stage algorithm (clustering + weighted regression/SGD) that unifies Hungarian-matching and K-means-based variants.

Non-trivial theoretical guarantees are provided for the affine case: exact optimality for Hungarian Fusion and a (9+ε)-approximation bound for K-means Fusion via a clean projection argument, which is more theoretical grounding than is typical in this literature.

The incorporation of neuron importance/attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the matching and loss is a reasonable and fairly novel idea, and the authors show it can be retrofitted into Git Re-Basin as well, somewhat strengthening the generality of the idea.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: non-IID (Dirichlet), sharded (disjoint-class), and full-dataset fusion regimes are tested on two different architectures (VGG11/CIFAR-10, ViT/CIFAR-100), with both zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluation, and ablations on importance scores and loss landscape visualization.

Reasonably forthright limitations discussion (hyperparameter sensitivity of the gradient variant, data-size dependence) and detailed appendices covering proofs, data partitioning, training/fusion hyperparameters, and runtime comparisons, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scale and generality claims are not well supported: despite claiming the method 'generalizes to arbitrary layer types' and works on 'any differentiable DNN architecture,' experiments are restricted to two relatively small vision architectures (VGG11, a small ViT) on CIFAR-10/100; no evidence is given for larger models, other modalities (e.g., language models), or more heterogeneous architectures, which undercuts the significance claims motivated in the introduction about large, data-hungry models.

Baseline coverage is incomplete and uneven: Hungarian Fusion and Git Re-Basin are reported as 'N/A' for 4-way and 8-way splits (Tables 1, 9, 11) because they are restricted to pairwise/one-to-one matching, leaving comparisons at higher model counts entirely to the authors' own K-means variants without a matching baseline, which weakens the strength of the comparative claims in the harder, more interesting regimes.

Potential evaluation bias: the paper selects and reports 'the result with the best-performing importance score' for its own methods (Section 5.2) without clarifying whether an analogous best-of-several selection procedure was applied to baselines (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin also use importance variants per Appendix C), raising concern about an apples-to-oranges comparison that could inflate the apparent advantage of the proposed method.

The strongest theoretical guarantees (Theorem 2) apply only to affine/linear levels, yet most of the actual experiments use the 'Gradient' K-means variant on non-linear architectures (ViT) where no such guarantee holds; this creates a meaningful gap between the theoretical contribution and the empirical method actually evaluated in the harder settings.

The comparison against a directly relevant and more modern baseline (Transformer OTFusion, Imfeld et al. 2023) is acknowledged to be unfair/incomplete: the authors could not adapt the official implementation and used a different (non-grid-searched) fine-tuning schedule than the original paper, undermining confidence in the one comparison that targets transformer-specific fusion.

Practical significance is tempered by the persistent large gap to ensembling across all tables (e.g., Table 1, 2, 8), and by the substantial runtime cost of the K-means Linear variant (~80s vs <1s for OTFusion in Table 6), with limited discussion of how this scales to larger networks or more models.

The method requires two very different, dataset/architecture-specific hyperparameter 'settings' (Table 5) chosen post hoc per experimental regime (e.g., Setting 1 vs Setting 2 for non-IID vs full-dataset), which suggests the gradient-based variant is not robustly self-tuning and may require nontrivial manual retuning for new settings, partially contradicting the practicality motivation of the paper.

The abstract leaves the code link blank/unspecified ('The code is available at:'), and no public repository URL is given in the text, which is a minor but real reproducibility concern for a paper that otherwise claims extensive open-source support.

strengths: Principled formulation: the paper decomposes the neuron-level fusion objective into interpretable grouping and approximation error terms (Theorem 1), giving a clean two-stage algorithmic recipe that is easy to reason about and instantiate differently (Hungarian vs K-means, linear vs gradient-based).

Theoretical guarantees are provided for both the pairwise equal-size case (exact optimality via the Hungarian algorithm) and the general multi-model case (a (9+epsilon)-approximation bound leveraging known K-means approximation results), which is a nontrivial, if largely combinatorial, contribution absent from prior fusion work.

Generality beyond linear layers: unlike OTFusion/Git Re-Basin (originally linear/activation-matching focused) the framework explicitly supports arbitrary differentiable layers via the gradient-based variant, and is demonstrated on both CNNs (VGG11) and Transformers (ViT).

The incorporation of neuron importance/attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the grouping/weighting step is a sensible and apparently effective addition, and the authors show it also improves existing baselines (Git Re-Basin) when retrofitted, strengthening the claim that saliency-aware fusion is broadly useful.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across three realistic regimes (Dirichlet non-IID, sharded/class-disjoint, and full-dataset with different seeds), two architectures/datasets (VGG11/CIFAR-10, ViT/CIFAR-100), with multiple splits (2/4/6/8-way) and 3-5 seeds with reported variance.

Useful ablations and diagnostics: clustering visualizations under different importance weightings, loss/accuracy landscape interpolation plots suggesting flatter minima for fused models, and runtime comparisons across methods.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility appendices (data partitioning formulas, training hyperparameters, fusion hyperparameter settings, proofs), which would aid replication alongside the promised code release.
weaknesses: The intended comparison to Transformer OTFusion (Imfeld et al. 2023), the most directly relevant baseline for ViT fusion, was dropped due to implementation difficulties, leaving the Transformer experiments without a strong, matched prior-art comparison beyond weaker baselines (KD, ensembling, vanilla averaging).

The gradient-based fusion variant (the only one applicable to non-linear/ViT settings) requires substantial, regime-specific hyperparameter tuning (two different 'Settings' selected per experiment type, as shown in Table 5 and the accompanying text), undermining claims of practicality and 'effectively regardless of training data distribution'; this is acknowledged as a limitation but is a significant practical caveat.

There is a non-trivial and sometimes large gap between the proposed fusion methods and the ensemble upper bound, especially in harder regimes (e.g., sharded ViT: ~49% vs ~62% ensemble, Table 2), which tempers the paper's framing that results 'approach ensemble-level performance.'

The motivation repeatedly invokes large-scale, data-hungry models (and even LLMs) trained on heterogeneous data, but all experiments are on relatively small CIFAR-10/100 classifiers (VGG11, small ViT); there is no evidence the method scales to the regimes that motivate the work, and runtime figures (e.g., K-means Linear Fusion taking ~80x longer than OTFusion) raise scalability concerns for larger numbers of clients/models.
Federated-learning baselines explicitly discussed in related work (FedAvg, FedMA) are not empirically compared against, despite non-IID/federated motivation being central to the paper's framing.

Baseline methods (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin) are only evaluated for 2-way splits and marked N/A beyond that due to their pairwise restriction; while this is a known limitation of those methods, it narrows the empirical comparison for larger numbers of parties to only the authors' own variants and weaker baselines (KD, averaging), making superiority claims in those regimes less contested.
The code repository link is not provided in the submitted manuscript (placeholder text), so independent verification of reproducibility is not currently possible from the paper alone.

The K-means approximation guarantee, while a nice touch, is a fairly direct application of an existing generic (9+epsilon)-approximation result for weighted K-means rather than a tailored novel analysis, and the bound itself is loose and may not be very informative in practice.

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical framework: fusion is cast as a representation-matching problem with a clean grouping-error/approximation-error decomposition (Theorem 1) and formal approximation guarantees for the proposed algorithms (Theorem 2, including a (9+ε)-approximation bound for K-means Fusion), which is more rigorous than most prior fusion heuristics.

Broad empirical validation spanning multiple architectures (VGG11, ResNets 18/34/50, ViT) and datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, BloodMNIST) and multiple realistic fusion regimes (full-dataset, non-IID, extreme sharded/class-disjoint, real-world medical imaging split).

Consistent and often large empirical gains over strong baselines (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, ZipIt!, KD, LP) precisely in the zero-shot/non-IID setting that the paper identifies as underexplored, including cases where baselines collapse to near-random accuracy while the proposed methods retain substantial accuracy.

Useful ablations and analyses: effect of neuron importance scoring on clustering (with quantitative Rand-index comparisons), sensitivity to fusion dataset size and mitigation via augmentation, robustness to different model widths, runtime breakdowns showing fusion overhead is small relative to fine-tuning, and a loss-landscape visualization supporting the claim of flatter fused minima.
Practical extension to model compression via retrofitting (teacher-to-smaller-student), showing meaningful gains over KD with limited data, broadening the applicability of the framework.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, runtime overhead) and provides an open-source reimplementation aimed at improving reproducibility across the field.
weaknesses: The gradient-based variants (HF/KF-Gradient), which perform best in many experiments, require per-level SGD over a labeled/representative fusion dataset for up to 100 epochs, which is a substantially heavier procedure than the label of "zero-shot" fusion suggests when compared to single-pass OT/permutation methods; this added cost and complexity is somewhat under-emphasized relative to the accuracy gains reported.

Theorem 2's guarantees hold only per-level with all preceding levels fixed (greedy composition); there is no analysis of how approximation/grouping errors compound across levels for deep networks, leaving the end-to-end quality of the fused model without formal guarantees.

Results are inconsistent regarding which variant (HF vs KF, Uniform vs Conductance vs DeepLIFT) is best across settings (e.g., Table 2, Table 18), and the paper does not offer principled guidance for a practitioner to select among these many variants a priori.

The claim of being architecture-agnostic ("any modularizable architecture") is only empirically validated on three closely related vision architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT); no experiments on other modalities (e.g., LLMs, RNNs, graph networks) are provided, despite this being highlighted as a key contribution.

Runtime costs for the linear variants (especially KF-Linear) are substantially higher than lightweight baselines (e.g., 78s vs 0.7s for OTFusion on VGG), and while the paper argues this is amortized against fine-tuning cost in full-dataset settings, this may not hold for very large-scale models where fusion itself could become a bottleneck.

The claim in the conclusion of being "the first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores" is in some tension with the paper's own discussion (Section C) that OTFusion already incorporates importance as a transport probability measure; the novelty framing could be more precise.

Some result tables (e.g., Table 2, Table 17) are dense and awkwardly formatted with multiple individual-model accuracies crammed together, reducing readability and making it harder to verify comparisons at a glance.

Direct empirical comparison with FL-specific baselines mentioned in the introduction (FedAvg, FedMA) is discussed conceptually but not included in the main quantitative benchmarks, despite the paper's framing around FL-relevant non-IID settings.

strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical decomposition (Theorem 1) of the representation-matching cost into grouping error and approximation error, with a full proof, which gives the method a principled foundation compared to prior heuristic matching-then-averaging approaches.

Theorem 2 provides concrete approximation guarantees (exact optimality for Hungarian Fusion under linear levels, and a (9+eps)-approximation for K-means Fusion), which is a nontrivial theoretical contribution largely absent from prior fusion literature.

Broad empirical coverage across three architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT), multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-1k, BloodMNIST), and three realistic data regimes (sharded, non-IID, full-dataset), which is more extensive than typical fusion papers.

The paper explicitly targets an underexplored and practically relevant gap: zero-shot fusion under heterogeneous/non-IID data, motivated by federated-learning-like constraints, and shows large, consistent gains over OTFusion/Git Re-Basin/ZipIt! in these regimes.

Good framing of KD and Linear Probing as special cases of the proposed framework, and a thoughtful ablation suite (importance-score effect on clustering, fusion dataset size, model width robustness, ResNet compression, loss-landscape visualization).
Transparent limitations and runtime discussion (Section F.5), including honest acknowledgment that gradient-based variants are slower and data-hungry, with reasonable mitigating arguments.
weaknesses: The gradient-based variants (HF/KF-Gradient) require substantial fusion data and up to 100 SGD epochs per level, which blurs the 'zero-shot, no retraining' narrative central to the paper's motivation; comparisons against training-free baselines like OTFusion/Git Re-Basin (which require no optimization at all) are therefore not entirely apples-to-apples, and the large runtime gap (e.g., 632s vs <1s) is only partially addressed by the fine-tuning-dominates argument.

Despite extensive motivation around federated learning and non-IID settings in the introduction and related work, FedAvg and FedMA are never included as experimental baselines in Section 5, leaving the comparison to FL-relevant methods incomplete.

Key recent related methods explicitly cited as addressing the same failure modes—REPAIR (Jordan et al., 2023) for zero-shot Re-Basin accuracy, and PLeaS (Nasery et al., 2025)—are discussed but never empirically compared against, weakening the significance claims relative to current state of the art.

The generality claim ('any architecture modularizable as a DAG of levels') is only validated on vision architectures (VGG, ResNet, ViT); no experiments on LLMs/transformer language models or other modalities are provided, despite this being highlighted as a key differentiator from prior work limited to specific architectures.

The theoretical guarantees (Theorem 2) hold only for a single level with all previous levels frozen; there is no end-to-end bound accounting for error accumulation across levels, which is acknowledged in the text but means the strongest theoretical claims do not actually certify quality of the final fused multi-level model.

Some experiments rely on a single seed (e.g., Table 18's 4-way ViT fusion) or very small sample sizes (e.g., BloodMNIST fusion with 400 samples), limiting statistical confidence in several headline numbers.

The hyperparameter configuration for gradient-based variants was tuned by the authors to 'generalize well' across the tested settings, but the process for arriving at this configuration is not fully transparent, raising reproducibility and potential cherry-picking concerns, especially since the paper itself notes sensitivity to hyperparameters as a limitation.

strengths: Principled theoretical framework: the paper decomposes the representation-matching cost into an interpretable 'grouping error' and 'approximation error' (Theorem 1), with a full proof, and builds a two-stage algorithm (clustering + weight fitting) directly from this decomposition.

Theoretical guarantees are provided for both algorithm variants: exact optimality for Hungarian Fusion under affine levels, and a (9+epsilon)-approximation bound for K-means Fusion via reduction to weighted k-means, which is unusual rigor for this line of work.

Broad architectural generality: the method is demonstrated on VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs (including with different widths/depths and >2 models), addressing a genuine gap where prior methods (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, ZipIt!) are restricted to specific architectures or pairwise fusion.

Extensive and varied empirical evaluation: sharded non-IID, Dirichlet non-IID, full-dataset, BloodMNIST (a realistic FL-like medical scenario), ImageNet-1k comparison with ZipIt!, model compression, and robustness studies (fusion dataset size, different widths, importance-score effects on clustering, loss landscape visualization).

Strong and consistent empirical gains specifically in the zero-shot/non-IID regime, where competing baselines (OTFusion, Transformer OTFusion, Git Re-Basin) often collapse to near-random accuracy while the proposed methods retain substantial accuracy without any fine-tuning.
Novel incorporation of neuron importance/saliency scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the fusion objective, shown to help both the proposed methods and, as a byproduct, improve Git Re-Basin.

Reproducibility focus: the authors provide an open-source, architecture-agnostic reimplementation intended to unify fragmented prior implementations and facilitate systematic benchmarking, along with detailed hyperparameter tables and runtime breakdowns in the appendix.

Honest limitations discussion (hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, runtime overhead) accompanied by concrete mitigations (data augmentation, runtime decomposition showing fine-tuning dominates cost in full-dataset settings).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees (Theorem 2) hold only for a single level with all preceding levels fixed; since the overall algorithm proceeds bottom-up greedily fixing earlier levels, there is no analysis of how approximation/grouping errors compound across levels, so the end-to-end quality guarantee for the full network is unclear.

No experiments on large language models or other NLP/sequence architectures despite claims of general applicability to any DAG-of-levels architecture; this is deferred entirely to future work, limiting the demonstrated scope of generality.

HF-Gradient/HF-Linear only apply to the restrictive two-model, equal-width, one-to-one matching case (marked N/A for >2-way splits in several tables), so a large fraction of the practically interesting results rely on the heuristic KF variants whose approximation guarantee is looser and whose practical performance sometimes trails HF in the 2-way setting.

The representation-cost objective being minimized is only a proxy for downstream task accuracy; while empirically it correlates with strong accuracy, there is no formal argument or analysis connecting the theoretical guarantees on representation cost to the reported accuracy gains.

Gradient-based variants require a non-trivial amount of fusion data (hundreds to thousands of samples) and are noticeably slower than lightweight baselines (e.g., KF-Linear is ~100x slower than OTFusion in Table 10); although the paper argues this is justified by enabling previously-unattainable zero-shot capability, this remains a practical constraint in very large-scale or latency-sensitive settings.

ResNet experiments are comparatively limited (ImageNet-1k sharded comparison and compression only) relative to the more extensive VGG/ViT experiments, despite ResNets being listed as a primary validated architecture family.

Some comparisons have overlapping confidence intervals among different importance-score variants (Uniform/Conductance/DeepLIFT), and no statistical significance testing is reported to substantiate claims that saliency-weighted variants reliably outperform uniform weighting.

Recently referenced related work such as PLeaS (Nasery et al., 2025) is cited but not empirically compared against, leaving open how the proposed method stacks up against the most recent alternatives.
